title: A Redirect Can Work Perfectly and Still Be Wrong. The Difference Is One Digit.
excerpt: One digit changed my HTTP status code. It worked for users but misled machines. Don't ignore the unseen layers. Check your status codes. They matter more than you think.
content:
Recently, I changed a single character in how my domain behaves.
Not the design. Not the content. Not a line of copy.
One digit in an HTTP status code.

To every visitor, nothing changed. The site loaded exactly as before. But to every search engine, crawler, and AI system reading the site, the meaning changed completely. What had been interpreted as a temporary arrangement became a permanent declaration.
That gap—between what humans see and what machines are told—is where a surprising amount of silent damage lives.
The Setup

Like many websites, my personal site has two possible front doors:
•	the bare domain
•	the same domain with "www" in front

Only one should be the authoritative version. The other should simply forward visitors to it.
Most people get this far. They configure the redirect, type the domain into a browser, arrive at the correct destination, and conclude the job is done.
I did too.
Then I inspected the actual HTTP response.
The redirect was returning a 307.

What Humans Never See

A 307 is a temporary redirect.
A 308 is a permanent redirect.

To a visitor, they are indistinguishable. Both land you on the same page. Both appear to work perfectly.
But machines don't read websites the way humans do.

They read intent.
A 307 tells a crawler: "Keep the original address around. This change may not be permanent."
A 308 tells it: "This move is final. Consolidate everything to the destination."

That distinction matters.

A temporary redirect can cause search engines and AI crawlers to continue treating both URLs as active candidates. Authority, trust signals, and indexing can remain split across two addresses.
A permanent redirect consolidates those signals onto the canonical destination.
In other words, the redirect was doing its visible job perfectly while quietly communicating the wrong story to every machine that mattered.

The fix?
One digit.
307 → 308.
No redesign. No migration. No new content strategy.
Just correcting the instruction being sent beneath the surface.
"Works for Me" Is Not a Valid Test
The lesson extends far beyond redirects.

Almost every system you operate has two audiences:
1.	The human using it.
2.	The machine interpreting it.

- Websites have visitors and crawlers.
- APIs have users and dependent services.
- Documents have readers and search indexes.
- Business processes have participants and reporting systems.

Naturally, we test for the audience we can see. The danger is that the invisible audience often makes the more consequential decisions.
The site loads. The page renders.Nothing appears broken.
Meanwhile, a machine is acting on a signal you never intended to send.

Those failures are expensive because they remain invisible from the only vantage point most operators ever check.
The discipline is simple but uncommon:
- Don't just verify that the redirect works.
- Verify what the redirect says.
- Don't just check that the page renders.
- Check what the crawler understands.

Passing the human test does not guarantee passing the machine test.

Why This Matters More in the AI Era?

A decade ago, the primary machine reading your site was a search engine.
The penalty for sending confusing signals was often a ranking issue.
Today, the machine reading your site may be an AI assistant answering questions about you, your company, or your work.
When someone asks an AI system who you are, where to find your work, or which website represents you, it relies on the same machine-readable infrastructure:
•	Canonical URLs
•	Redirects
•	Structured signals
•	Consistency across domains

Ambiguous signals create ambiguous answers.
Two partially authoritative domains create two competing identities.
And when a machine cannot confidently determine the authoritative version, it either hedges or guesses.
Neither outcome serves you.
The infrastructure layer that once felt like a technical footnote is increasingly becoming the foundation of digital reputation.
The status code is no longer a webmaster detail.
It is part of how machines decide what is true.

The Operator's Lesson

Large institutions have entire teams dedicated to machine-readable systems.
They monitor infrastructure, metadata, redirects, indexing behavior, schemas, APIs, and machine-facing surfaces because they understand that what machines see eventually shapes what people see.

A solo operator gets none of those defaults for free.

You either build that habit deliberately, or you discover the consequences later.
The afternoon I spent identifying and correcting one digit was inexpensive.
The alternative—allowing a split signal to persist for months while wondering why authority wasn't consolidating—would have been far more costly.

The redirect was a small example of a larger rule:
Invisible errors often create visible consequences.
And the longer they remain unseen, the more expensive they become.

If you run anything online, don't just check where your domain sends people. Check what it tells machines.

Those are not the same thing. And increasingly, the second matters more than the first.
